B12_00: Inner ear development in the vertebrate embryo, when the earliest precursor of the hearing and balance organs forms from surface tissue of the head. Because the cochlea, vestibular organs and their sensory cells all derive from it, disruption at this stage causes profound congenital deafness and balance defects, sometimes within syndromes that also affect the retina and kidney.
B12_01: Early embryonic development during gastrulation, when cells adopt the germ-layer identity that later gives rise to the gut, liver, pancreas and lung epithelium. Correct timing and placement matter because errors leave organ primordia mispositioned or missing. The influences involved tune how often cells take this route rather than dictate it, shaping the size and placement of the future digestive and respiratory organs.
B12_02: Vertebrate embryonic trunk development, where the tissue on either side of the future spine is divided into repeating segments that later form vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis. The pace and regularity of this segmentation matter: when disturbed, segments become irregular, fused or asymmetric, the developmental origin of congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis.
B12_03: Embryonic heart development, concerning a pool of precursor cells in the lateral mesoderm, separate from the first heart field, that builds most of the right ventricle, the outflow tract at the arterial pole and part of the inflow region. These are exactly the structures affected in conotruncal and right-sided congenital heart disease, including tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle and persistent truncus arteriosus.
B12_04: Early kidney development in the embryo, at the moment the duct draining the primitive kidney first sends an outgrowth toward the kidney-forming mesenchyme. Everything downstream depends on it, since the outgrowth becomes the collecting duct system and induces nephrons. Failure or misplaced budding causes renal agenesis, hypoplasia, duplex kidneys and vesicoureteric reflux, central forms of congenital kidney and urinary tract anomaly.
B12_05: Vertebrate embryonic trunk development, in which each body segment is divided into front and back halves before any visible boundary appears. This organisation later decides where vertebrae form relative to muscle and which corridors migrating neural crest cells and motor nerves follow. Its loss produces fused and malformed vertebrae and disordered spinal nerve segmentation, as seen in congenital spine disorders.
B12_06: Development of ducts that connect secretory organs to a body surface, including sweat and salivary glands, mammary ducts and airways, in which a solid cord of cells is hollowed into an open channel. Failure leaves blind or blocked ducts with loss of secretion. Its disruption in skin appendages underlies hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, in which sweat glands lack usable openings and affected people cannot sweat normally.
B12_07: Embryonic organ development, concerning the cues that promote formation of the epithelial and endothelial tubes making up kidney nephrons, airways, glands and blood vessels. Kidney development is especially prominent, from the first ureteric outgrowth to specification of nephron-forming tissue. Loss of these inputs causes renal agenesis or hypoplasia, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, and defective formation of vessels and glandular ducts.
B12_08: Male germ cell development in the testis, during the final shaping of spermatids into mature sperm, when the cap-like structure covering the front of the sperm head is built. This structure is what lets sperm penetrate the egg's coat and fuse with it at fertilisation. Its absence produces round-headed sperm (globozoospermia), a recognised cause of male infertility that can be overcome only by assisted fertilisation.
B12_09: Brain and spinal cord white matter, where oligodendrocytes wrap axons with an insulating sheath during neural development. This sheath enables fast nerve conduction along white matter tracts and supports the long-term health of axons. Failure to form or maintain it underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, linking glial development to neurological function.
B12_10: Gastrulation in the early embryo, when epiblast cells decide whether to become mesoderm, setting how much of this germ layer forms, where and when. Its outcome determines the heart, blood, skeleton and muscle; misregulation produces axis duplication, failed primitive streak formation or missing cardiac progenitors. The same decision is steered when pluripotent stem cells are directed into mesodermal lineages in culture.
B12_11: Early development of the vertebrate central nervous system, when the flat neural plate of the embryo rises at its edges into a groove whose margins later meet to form the neural tube. If this shaping fails, the tube cannot close, producing neural tube defects such as exencephaly, anencephaly or spina bifida. It involves both the neuroepithelium and the overlying surface ectoderm.
B12_12: Early embryonic development, at the stage when cells become competent, though not yet irreversibly committed, to form endoderm, the germ layer giving rise to gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid. Failures here compromise the entire digestive and respiratory lineage. The same programme is used to derive definitive endoderm from pluripotent stem cells in culture, which matters for regenerative medicine.
B12_13: Heart muscle development, concerning how embryonic cardiomyocytes build the ordered contractile apparatus that lets the heart beat. Without it the embryonic heart cannot generate organised force. In the adult heart, defective building or maintenance of this apparatus underlies dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, so the process connects cardiomyocyte differentiation and growth to lifelong cardiac function.
B12_14: Development of the airway in the embryo, as the trachea is separated from the oesophagus out of the anterior foregut and connected to the bronchi below. Its success determines whether a newborn can breathe and swallow independently. Failure produces tracheoesophageal fistula, oesophageal atresia, tracheal agenesis or stenosis, and tracheomalacia when the supporting cartilage rings are malformed.
B12_15: Vertebrate trunk development, when each newly formed body segment acquires its own positional identity, fixing which vertebra, rib and body-wall muscle group will come from it. Errors produce fused or malformed vertebrae and rib defects of the kind seen in congenital segmentation disorders of the spine. It bridges early periodic patterning of the embryo and the later axial skeleton and musculature.
B12_16: Skeletal muscle fibres during development and regeneration, where the contractile units must be built with the right geometry to generate force. Failure causes nemaline myopathy, a congenital muscle disease with disorganised, rod-containing fibres and severe weakness, often presenting in infancy. The process matters both for muscle formation in the embryo and for repair of damaged fibres later in life.
B12_17: Embryonic organ formation, in which one tissue, typically an epithelium, signals to a neighbouring mesenchyme and commits a field of cells to build an organ such as the kidney, limb, lung, heart or gonad. These interactions decide where organs arise and how large they become. Loss or misplacement of such signals produces organ agenesis, hypoplasia and congenital malformations.
B12_18: Development of the prostate in the male fetus, where buds of epithelium grow from the urogenital sinus under male hormonal control. This determines how many buds form, prostate size and its branching architecture; failure gives prostatic agenesis or hypoplasia. The same developmental programmes reawaken in adult men in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer, making the process clinically relevant beyond development.
B12_19: Early development of the urinary and male reproductive tracts, when the duct draining the primitive kidney first forms and extends to join the cloaca. From it arise the ureter, the collecting system and, in males, parts of the reproductive tract. Failure or misrouting causes renal agenesis, duplex or ectopic ureters and vesicoureteral reflux, and underlies inherited renal-coloboma and renal cyst syndromes.
B12_20: Vertebrate embryos building the trunk and tail progressively from a progenitor zone at the tail end, extending the body axis so that segments can be added one after another. Without this growth the axis is truncated, fewer segments form, and the vertebrae, ribs and axial muscles derived from them are incomplete. It ties tail-bud progenitor maintenance to the timing of body segmentation.
B12_21: Kidney development, at the point where nephron-forming cells of the embryonic metanephros first organise into the tube that becomes the nephron's filtering and reabsorbing segments. Failure leaves nephrons unformed, causing renal hypoplasia, dysplasia or agenesis. Even partial deficits reduce nephron endowment at birth, which predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease later in life.
B12_22: Embryonic heart development, concerning how long a pool of dividing cardiac precursors in the second heart field keeps proliferating before maturing, which sets the size of the right ventricle, outflow tract and inflow region. Too little expansion underlies outflow tract malformations such as persistent truncus arteriosus and double outlet right ventricle, and contributes to underdeveloped right-sided chambers.
B12_23: Embryonic closure of epithelial folds into sealed tubes, most importantly the neural tube that forms the brain and spinal cord, but also the optic fissure of the eye and the palate. Failure produces some of the commonest human birth defects: spina bifida, anencephaly and craniorachischisis. Maternal vitamin status influences risk, which is why periconceptional supplementation prevents many cases.
B12_24: Gastrulation in the vertebrate embryo, when cells leaving the primitive streak are allocated to the band of tissue flanking the neural tube rather than to lateral or intermediate fates. This band later segments and gives rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis, establishing the segmented trunk. Defects in its formation produce axial skeletal and vascular abnormalities.
B12_25: Striated muscle, particularly the heart, where contractile units are built as cardiomyocytes mature and as the heart enlarges in response to increased workload. The focus is on the upstream cues that encourage this construction rather than its building blocks. When assembly and alignment fail, ventricular walls are thin and contract poorly, as in dilated cardiomyopathy.
B12_26: Myelinated nerve fibres of the central and peripheral nervous system, at the junctions flanking each node of Ranvier where the myelin sheath seals against the axon. These seals keep the electrical compartments of the fibre separate and enable fast, saltatory conduction. Their disruption slows conduction, disorganises nodes and causes severe congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy in infants.
